title: Bayes' rule: updating beliefs
summary: Bayes' rule turns P(evidence | hypothesis) into P(hypothesis | evidence) by weighting with the prior and dividing by the overall probability of the evidence. With a rare disease, even an accurate test leaves a positive result far from certain, and repeated evidence moves the belief step by step.
llm_link: A language model computes P(next token | everything before). Each extra word in the prompt is new evidence that reshapes that conditional distribution, much as evidence turns a prior into a posterior.
key_ideas: P(H | E) = P(E | H) · P(H) / P(E): posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.
P(E) = P(E | H)·P(H) + P(E | not H)·P(not H): add up every way the evidence can happen.
P(E | H) and P(H | E) are different questions; confusing them is the classic mistake.
Today's posterior is tomorrow's prior: independent pieces of evidence can be applied one after another.

quiz.q: Predict the result: prevalence 1%, the test catches 99% of the ill and falsely flags 1% of the healthy. You test positive. P(ill | +) is closest to…
quiz.explain: Out of 10,000 people: 99 true positives and 99 false positives, so half of the 198 positives are ill. (0.99·0.01) / (0.99·0.01 + 0.01·0.99) = 0.5.

quiz.q: Same test, but the disease affects 1 in 10 people. What happens to P(ill | +)?
quiz.explain: A larger prior means the true positives outnumber the false alarms: 0.099 / (0.099 + 0.009) ≈ 0.92.

quiz.q: Which quantity does a test's "99% accuracy on sick patients" describe?
quiz.explain: It is the probability of a positive result given illness, the likelihood. What a patient wants is the reverse, P(ill | +).

quiz.q: After one positive result your belief is 0.5. A second, independent positive test (same accuracy) arrives. The new belief is about…
A language model reads "The capital of France is". In Bayesian terms, what do the words of the prompt act like?
options: Evidence that reshapes the distribution over the next token
quiz.explain: The model outputs P(next token | context). Each extra word of context changes that conditional distribution, here concentrating it on "Paris".

problems.title: A Bayes calculator
problems.prompt:
Write posterior(prior, sens, fpr): the probability of being ill after a positive test, where

  • prior = P(ill)
  • sens = P(+ | ill), the sensitivity
  • fpr = P(+ | healthy), the false-positive rate

First compute the evidence P(+) = sens·prior + fpr·(1 − prior), then apply Bayes' rule.

posterior(0.10, 0.99, 0.01)   # 0.9166...

tests.name: the rare-disease puzzle
tests.code:
out = posterior(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)
assert out is not None, 'posterior returned None'
assert abs(out - 0.5) < 1e-9, f'expected 0.5 (99 true positives vs 99 false alarms), got {out}'

tests.name: a common disease
tests.code:
out = posterior(0.10, 0.99, 0.01)
assert abs(out - 0.099 / 0.108) < 1e-9, f'expected about 0.917, got {out}. Check P(+) = sens*prior + fpr*(1 - prior)'

tests.name: not the likelihood
tests.code:
out = posterior(0.001, 0.99, 0.01)
assert out < 0.1, f'with a 1-in-1000 prior a positive test is still probably a false alarm (about 0.09); got {out}. Did you return sens instead of P(ill | +)?'

tests.name: a perfect test
tests.code:
out = posterior(0.01, 1.0, 0.0)
assert abs(out - 1.0) < 1e-9, f'with no false positives, a positive result means certainly ill; got {out}'

problems.title: Belief after several tests
problems.prompt:
Write update_all(prior, results, sens, fpr). results is a list of test outcomes, True for positive and False for negative. Apply Bayes' rule once per result, using each posterior as the next prior, and return the final belief.

For a negative result the likelihoods change: P(− | ill) = 1 − sens and P(− | healthy) = 1 − fpr.

update_all(0.01, [True, True], 0.99, 0.01)   # 0.99
update_all(0.5, [False], 0.99, 0.01)         # 0.01

tests.name: no tests, no change
tests.code:
out = update_all(0.3, [], 0.9, 0.1)
assert abs(out - 0.3) < 1e-9, f'with no evidence the belief should stay at the prior 0.3, got {out}'

tests.name: two positives
tests.code:
out = update_all(0.01, [True, True], 0.99, 0.01)
assert abs(out - 0.99) < 1e-9, f'first test gives 0.5, the second should give 0.99; got {out}. Are you feeding each posterior back in as the prior?'

tests.name: a negative result
tests.code:
out = update_all(0.5, [False], 0.99, 0.01)
assert abs(out - 0.01) < 1e-9, f'a negative result uses 1 - sens and 1 - fpr: 0.01*0.5 / (0.01*0.5 + 0.99*0.5) = 0.01, got {out}'

tests.name: order does not matter
tests.code:
a = update_all(0.2, [True, False, True], 0.8, 0.1)
b = update_all(0.2, [True, True, False], 0.8, 0.1)
assert abs(a - b) < 1e-9, f'independent evidence gives the same answer in any order, got {a} and {b}'

problems.title: Posterior for many priors at once (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Redo posterior so that prior can be a NumPy array of priors. Because +, *, / and 1 - prior all work entry by entry on arrays, the same formula returns an array of posteriors with the same shape: this is the curve from the video.

priors = np.array([0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1])
posterior_curve(priors, 0.99, 0.01)
# array([0.0098, 0.0902, 0.5   , 0.9167])  (rounded)

tests.name: matches the scalar formula
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1])
out = posterior_curve(p, 0.99, 0.01)
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
exp = 0.99 * p / (0.99 * p + 0.01 * (1 - p))
assert np.allclose(out, exp), f'expected {np.round(exp, 4)}, got {out}'

tests.name: same shape as the input
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 7)
out = posterior_curve(p, 0.9, 0.2)
assert isinstance(out, np.ndarray) and out.shape == (7,), f'expected an array of shape (7,), got {type(out).__name__} {getattr(out, "shape", None)}. Avoid Python loops and lists: write the formula with array arithmetic'

tests.name: rises with the prior
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = posterior_curve(np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 50), 0.99, 0.01)
assert np.all(np.diff(out) > 0), 'a larger prior should always give a larger posterior for the same positive test'

hints: evidence = sens * priors + fpr * (1 - priors) is already an array.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def posterior_curve(priors, sens, fpr):
    evidence = sens * priors + fpr * (1 - priors)
    return sens * priors / evidence
